lessonTitle: Managing Multimorbidity: Priorities, Medication Review and Shared Decisions

blocks.text: A 78-year-old man lives with heart failure, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, COPD, osteoarthritis and depression. He takes fourteen regular medicines, sees five different clinics and has had three falls this year. Each specialist has followed their own guideline correctly. When you ask him what matters most, he says he wants to keep walking his dog and does not want to be in hospital again.

blocks.markdown: **Multimorbidity** is the presence of two or more long-term conditions in the same person. It is the norm rather than the exception in older patients and in deprived populations, and it is associated with poorer quality of life, greater treatment burden, higher mortality and more emergency admissions. Clinical guidelines and trials are mostly written for single diseases and often exclude people with several, so adding each guideline's recommendations together produces long medication lists, conflicting advice and a heavy burden of appointments and monitoring. NICE guideline NG56 describes a person-centred approach that this unit follows.

blocks.title: Treatment burden and polypharmacy
blocks.text: **Treatment burden** is the workload of healthcare imposed on a patient: taking medicines, attending appointments, monitoring, lifestyle changes and coordinating care. **Polypharmacy** is the use of multiple medicines, often defined as five or more; it becomes **problematic** when the medicines are not clinically indicated, not achieving the intended benefit or are causing harm. NICE suggests considering the multimorbidity approach in people who have, for example, difficulty managing treatments, receive care from multiple services, have both long-term physical and mental health conditions, frailty, or are prescribed many regular medicines (check current NICE NG56).

blocks.markdown: **Prioritising problems.** Prioritisation begins with the person, not the disease. Explore what matters to them (their goals, values, daily activities, worries and what they are willing to accept), then weigh this with clinical factors: which conditions and treatments pose the greatest risk to life or function now, which problems cause the most distress or disability, how interactions between conditions work, and which have a time to benefit that fits the person's prognosis. Agree a small number of shared priorities, name a **single coordinating clinician** where possible for continuity, and plan how reviews will be combined so that appointments and tests are minimised.

blocks.title: Prioritising for one patient
blocks.prompt: The patient in the hook has heart failure, diabetes, CKD, COPD, osteoarthritis and depression, and three recent falls. He wants to keep walking his dog and avoid admission. How would you prioritise?

steps.text: Ask what matters most: staying independent and out of hospital, with walking as the key activity. This frames priorities as function and avoiding admission.
List the problems threatening those goals: falls (injury, loss of confidence), breathlessness (heart failure and COPD), pain limiting walking (osteoarthritis), and low mood.

Review whether medicines contribute: blood pressure lowering and diuretics may cause postural hypotension, sedatives and some antidepressants raise falls risk, and tight glycaemic control with insulin or sulfonylureas risks hypoglycaemia.

Agree two or three shared priorities, such as reducing falls, optimising symptom control for breathlessness and pain, and treating low mood. Relax lower-value targets (for example very tight HbA1c) if they add risk, and arrange one structured review with a named clinician.

blocks.answer: Priorities are set by his goals (independence and no admissions): falls, symptom control and mood come before tight targets for individual diseases.

blocks.markdown: **Reviewing a medication list.** Use a structured method: for each medicine ask what the indication is, whether it is still needed and whether it is working; whether it is causing harm or interacting with another medicine or a condition (kidney function matters for many drugs); whether the dose is appropriate; whether a simpler regimen is possible; and whether the patient actually takes it and is willing to continue. Tools such as STOPP/START criteria support the review. **Deprescribing** means planned, supervised withdrawal of medicines whose harms outweigh benefits, done one change at a time with monitoring for relapse, and always discussed with the patient. Check any anticholinergic or sedative burden, renal dosing and duplicate therapies.

blocks.title: Medication review
blocks.prompt: An 82-year-old woman takes amlodipine, ramipril, bendroflumethiazide, a daily NSAID for osteoarthritis, a benzodiazepine for sleep, and an oral antihistamine for itch. Her creatinine has risen and she has fallen twice. What problems does the review reveal?

steps.text: ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID: the triple combination that can cause acute kidney injury, consistent with the raised creatinine.

NSAID in an older patient with hypertension and kidney impairment: raises blood pressure, renal risk and gastrointestinal bleeding risk; consider stopping and using safer analgesia such as paracetamol or topical treatment.
Benzodiazepine and sedating antihistamine: both sedative and anticholinergic burden, contributing to the falls and confusion.

Plan: stop the NSAID first, check renal function and electrolytes, taper the benzodiazepine slowly, review the antihistamine, and recheck blood pressure and falls risk. Make one change at a time and review in a short interval, with the patient's agreement.

blocks.answer: The NSAID with ACE inhibitor and diuretic threatens the kidneys; sedatives drive falls; stop the NSAID and plan a supervised taper of the sedatives.

blocks.markdown: **Competing risks and time to benefit.** In multimorbidity, a person may die or lose function from a different condition before the long-term benefit of a preventive treatment can be realised. A treatment whose benefit takes years to appear (for example a statin for primary prevention) is worth less to someone with a short life expectancy than to someone with decades ahead, while its burden and harms occur immediately. Trial results give an average effect in selected people, so for an individual we estimate absolute benefit, time to benefit, harm and burden, and then relate them to the person's goals.

blocks.caption: NNT = number needed to treat (people treated for the stated period for one to benefit); ARR = absolute risk reduction, expressed as a proportion over the same time period.

items: Share information in plain language: the condition, options (including doing nothing), realistic benefits and harms of each, and the uncertainty.
Present absolute risks and numbers needed to treat, and the time over which benefit accrues, rather than relative risk alone.
Elicit values and preferences: what the person wants to avoid or preserve (independence, avoiding hospital, symptom control).
Account for competing risks, frailty and cognition; check understanding and capacity; involve family or carers as the patient wishes.
Agree a decision, document it, and plan review; it is acceptable to decide to stop or not to start a treatment.
Remember that in the UK the person must be told about material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery) and may refuse.

blocks.title: Burden, benefit and values
blocks.text: Each additional medicine, test and appointment has a cost to the patient. A decision is good if it fits the person's values and realistic prognosis, not merely if it follows a guideline. The aim is the best achievable function and quality of life, with fewer, better-chosen interventions.

points: Multimorbidity (two or more long-term conditions) requires prioritising problems around what matters to the person, minimising treatment burden and providing coordinated care with a named clinician.

Medication review asks indication, benefit, harm, interactions, dose and adherence for each drug, identifies prescribing cascades and high-risk combinations (such as ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID), and deprescribes stepwise.
Shared decision-making weighs absolute benefit, time to benefit, harm and competing risks against the person's goals, using plain absolute numbers such as NNT.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has COPD, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis and depression and finds her treatments overwhelming. What is the most appropriate first step in prioritising her care?

options.text: Treat each condition strictly in line with its own disease guideline, one after another
Explore what matters most to her and her treatment burden, then agree a small number of shared priorities
Refer to a different specialist for each condition
Stop all medicines for one month

questions.correctOptionText: Explore what matters most to her and her treatment burden, then agree a small number of shared priorities

distractorRationale.a: Applying each guideline additively increases burden and conflict and ignores her goals.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: person-centred prioritisation starts with goals and burden.
distractorRationale.c: Separate referrals fragment care and add burden.
distractorRationale.d: Abrupt withdrawal of all medicines is unsafe.

questions.explanation: In multimorbidity the starting point is what matters to the person, and how much treatment burden they can manage. Priorities are then agreed collaboratively and coordinated, rather than following each disease guideline in isolation.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man is under six specialist clinics with eight long-term conditions and often misses appointments because of tiredness. Which strategy best reflects good multimorbidity care?

options.text: Appoint a named coordinating clinician and combine reviews to reduce appointments and tests

questions.correctOptionText: Appoint a named coordinating clinician and combine reviews to reduce appointments and tests

distractorRationale.b: Correct: continuity and consolidation of reviews reduce treatment burden.
distractorRationale.c: Discharging without review leaves risks unmanaged.
distractorRationale.d: Stopping all monitoring removes safety checks without discussion.

questions.explanation: High treatment burden is reduced by a named coordinating clinician, consolidated reviews and agreed priorities. Removing all care is not the aim; rationalising it is.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman with heart failure takes ramipril and spironolactone. She is given trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Five days later she is weak, her serum potassium is 6.8 mmol/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves. What best explains this?

options.text: Additive reduction of renal potassium excretion by an ACE inhibitor, spironolactone and trimethoprim

questions.correctOptionText: Additive reduction of renal potassium excretion by an ACE inhibitor, spironolactone and trimethoprim

distractorRationale.a: The potassium is high, not low.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: each of the three drugs reduces renal potassium excretion, so together they cause hyperkalaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Over-hydration does not cause this ECG picture.
distractorRationale.d: Weakness and ECG changes show this is a real clinical problem.

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics and trimethoprim each impair renal potassium excretion, so their combination in an older patient with reduced renal function can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia. The interaction should be recognised at prescribing, and an alternative antibiotic chosen.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman started amlodipine for hypertension and a few weeks later developed ankle swelling, for which furosemide was prescribed. She then developed postural dizziness and a fall. Which term best describes the sequence?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a side effect (oedema from amlodipine) was treated as a new condition with another drug.
distractorRationale.b: Tolerance is a diminished response over time.
distractorRationale.c: Polypharmacy here is harmful, not beneficial.
distractorRationale.d: There is no placebo mechanism in the stem.

questions.explanation: Amlodipine commonly causes ankle oedema. Treating that side effect with a diuretic is a prescribing cascade, which adds a new drug and new harms (such as postural hypotension and falls) rather than addressing the cause.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old man with advanced COPD, frailty and an estimated life expectancy of about 1 year is offered a new statin for primary prevention. Which approach best reflects shared decision-making with competing risks?

options.text: Start the statin because the guideline recommends it
Discuss the small absolute benefit, the years it takes to appear, the burden and harms, and what matters to him, and agree whether to start
Refuse to discuss prevention at all

questions.correctOptionText: Discuss the small absolute benefit, the years it takes to appear, the burden and harms, and what matters to him, and agree whether to start

distractorRationale.a: A guideline for the general population may not fit a patient with a short life expectancy.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: benefit takes years to appear, so it must be weighed with his prognosis and wishes.
distractorRationale.c: Decisions should be shared, not unilateral.
distractorRationale.d: Avoiding discussion removes his chance to choose.

questions.explanation: Statins for primary prevention have a time to benefit of years. For a frail patient with a short life expectancy the benefit may not materialise, while burden and harms are immediate, so the decision depends on his values and a clear explanation.

questions.stem: When deprescribing, it is usually safest to stop several medicines at once so that side effects can be assessed together.
questions.explanation: Changes are made one at a time so that benefits, harms and withdrawal effects can be attributed to a specific drug. Some drugs also need a gradual taper rather than abrupt withdrawal.

questions.stem: A trial reports a 5-year risk of a cardiovascular event of 8.0 percent without treatment and 5.5 percent with treatment. Calculate the number needed to treat (NNT) for 5 years to prevent one event.
questions.explanation: ARR = 8.0% - 5.5% = 2.5% = 0.025. NNT = 1/0.025 = 40. So 40 people must be treated for 5 years for one to avoid an event; the other 39 take the medicine and its burden without benefit from this outcome.

questions.stem: Explain how you would prioritise problems in a patient with several chronic conditions and a high treatment burden.
markingGuide: Elicit what matters to the patient: goals, values, daily activities, concerns
Identify problems that threaten those goals or life, cause most distress or disability, and interactions between conditions
Consider prognosis and time to benefit of each treatment
Agree a small number of shared priorities and relax low-value targets if they add risk or burden
Identify a named coordinating clinician and combine reviews to reduce appointments
Document the plan and review it
questions.explanation: Prioritisation is person-centred rather than disease-centred. The aim is to improve what matters while reducing burden, using clinical judgement about risk and benefit.

questions.stem: Describe a structured approach to reviewing a medication list in an older patient with multimorbidity and polypharmacy, including interactions and deprescribing.
markingGuide: For each drug: indication, benefit, harm, dose, renal function, adherence and patient preference
Identify interactions and high-risk combinations, such as ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID, NSAID + anticoagulant, multiple sedatives or anticholinergics
Recognise prescribing cascades and duplicate therapy
Deprescribe stepwise: one change at a time, taper where needed, monitor and review, with the patient's agreement
Consider the patient's goals and prognosis; check BNF and pharmacy advice
questions.explanation: A structured review turns a long list into a justified regimen, reducing harm and burden while preserving treatments with real benefit.

questions.stem: Explain how shared decision-making is conducted when a person has competing risks, using absolute risk and time to benefit in your answer.
markingGuide: Explain the options including no treatment, with benefits and harms in plain language
Use absolute risks and NNT rather than relative risk; relate the time to benefit to likely prognosis
Competing risks: death or disability from another condition may occur before long-term benefits appear; harms and burden are immediate
Elicit the patient's values and preferences, check understanding and capacity, involve carers as the patient wishes
Agree and document the decision, including a decision to stop or not start treatment; review
UK legal standard: disclose material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery)
questions.explanation: Shared decisions weigh quantified benefit against burden and prognosis in light of the person's values. Absolute numbers and time frames make that trade-off visible.
